title: Focused Finish: MGCs Aimed at Purpose, Goals, and Growth
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. offers a concrete, step-by-step example of a Focused Finish mini-project built around Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs), Strategy #1 in The Will to Learn. He has students respond to a Canvas writing assignment titled 'Who You Are, Where You're Going, and What You're Doing to Get There' during their normal 10-minute warm-up writing time, then uses those responses as the basis for brief one-on-one check-ins he conducts by pulling students aside during independent practice. He describes reading each student's writing beforehand so the conversation can be specific and personal, with particular attention to questions about purpose and meaning, which he says matter more now given what he calls the student motivation apocalypse. Stuart frames the whole project through a SMART goal, a can't-miss goal, and a moonshot goal, arguing this three-tier goal structure simultaneously builds the Effort, Efficacy, and Value beliefs in the teacher doing the project, not just the students receiving it.
points: A single Canvas writing prompt ('Who You Are, Where You're Going, and What You're Doing to Get There') doubles as both a Values Affirmation exercise and the raw material for personalized MGC check-ins.

Reading a student's own writing before pulling them aside lets Stuart ask specific, individualized questions rather than generic ones, making the two-minute check-in feel targeted rather than routine.
Framing an end-of-year project with a SMART goal, a can't-miss goal, and a moonshot goal simultaneously cultivates Effort, Efficacy, and Value beliefs in the teacher, not only in students.

Purpose-oriented questions are given special weight because, in Stuart's view, the 'student motivation apocalypse' has made purpose and meaning more powerful motivators than they've historically been.
The project is deliberately low-tech and low-prep — a printed clipboard sheet and one to two pull-asides per class period — showing that a meaningful MGC push doesn't require an elaborate system.
quotes: If I wanted to move my MGC game forward one more click between now and year's end, what would I do? Well as it happens, I've got a mini-project going right now toward that end. It is very simple.
Before pulling a student aside, I read what they wrote in Canvas. About 90% of the time, they'll have written something that helps me know what to say or ask about.
I've been especially drawn to the questions like that last one regarding purpose, as the student motivation apocalypse is making purpose and meaning even more powerful than they've always been.

You're doing something you believe is important, something that will move your teacher skill forward, expand your soul, deepen your practice. You've chosen it based on where you are today, not where you were at year's beginning or middle.

Can't-miss goal: Learn something about a student or about teaching. Literally impossible to miss this goal when you attempt to connect with 134 students, provided that you're doing so with at least a bit of mindfulness and presence at least some of the time.
These three kinds of goals are tremendous at cultivating the Five Key Beliefs in your own soul. The moonshot goal helps with Value; the can't-miss goal locks in Efficacy; the SMART goal grows Effort.
